lead: High-throughput computing (HTC) pushes many independent tasks through a pool of workers and counts work finished per hour. A team resizing a lakh of photos overnight cares only about the completed total. Each task is short, needs no other task, and can run on any free worker. The platform keeps every worker busy; an idle worker is lost throughput.
prereq: You need Chapter 5.1 for parallel and distributed programming models, especially master-worker.

sections.h3: HTC versus HPC, and the numbers that matter

blocks.text: High-performance computing (HPC) makes one tightly coupled job finish fast, so latency is the target. HTC runs many independent tasks and counts finished work per unit time, so throughput is the target. A bag-of-tasks application is N tasks with no dependencies and no messages: rendering frames, resizing photos, sweeping parameters.

blocks.where: N tasks; t minutes per task on a worker; o minutes of scheduling overhead the worker pays per task; W workers; T makespan in minutes. This holds when N divides evenly by W; otherwise round tasks per worker up.
N tasks; T makespan in minutes; throughput in tasks per minute.

sections.h3: Task models and the dependency DAG

blocks.text: A task is the unit of work: input files, one program, output files. In the task-based model the programmer writes the task only; the platform picks a worker, moves files, retries failures, collects results.

When task v needs task u's output, draw edge u → v. All edges form a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Independent tasks are a DAG with no edges. The makespan cannot be shorter than the longest path, the critical path.

Master-worker scheduling fits both. One master holds a queue of ready tasks; each worker takes one, runs it, reports back. If a worker dies the master re-issues that task, so tasks must be safe to repeat. Tasks are kept small, and each worker holds only a small batch at a time, so one slow task delays very little work and the other workers stay busy.

Aneka is a .NET platform for running .NET and Java applications on a private or public cloud. You describe each task, submit the set to an AnekaApplication, and Aneka's master places tasks on worker nodes. Only a few universities teach this in depth.

items: Write a task class overriding Execute; read inputs from the task's file data.
Create AnekaApplication with the task type and a config file naming the master.
Add tasks; call AddDependency when one task needs another's output.
Submit and wait; Aneka stages inputs out and results back.
Read results from task objects or output files.

blocks.text: Because the programmer never names a worker, Aneka can grow the pool or move a task after failure without code changes.

figure.caption: Each of the 12 workers runs 50 tasks, 200 minutes of work plus 25 minutes of scheduling overhead, so the run ends at 225 minutes and the throughput is about 2.67 tasks a minute.

spec.aria: Twelve worker lanes, each a 200-minute work bar followed by a 25-minute overhead bar, all ending together at 225 minutes.

examples.question: 600 independent tasks, each 4 min on any worker. 12 workers. Scheduling costs 0.5 min per task, paid by the worker. Find ideal makespan, actual makespan and throughput.
examples.answer: Ideal 200 min, actual 225 min, throughput 2.67 tasks/min.
examples.check:
N = 600
t = 4
o = 0.5
W = 12
per_worker = N / W
ideal = per_worker * t
actual = per_worker * (t + o)
throughput = N / actual
print(int(ideal))
print(int(actual))
print(round(throughput, 2))

traps: HTC maximises tasks per minute; HPC maximises speed of one job. Latency questions belong to HPC.
Overhead is per task per worker. Total overhead 600 × 0.5 = 300 min of worker-time is only 25 min on each of 12 workers; do not subtract 300 from makespan.

Adding workers stops helping when a shared resource becomes the bottleneck: the master that hands out tasks, the shared file store, or the network. Each worker's own ceiling is 1 ÷ (t + o) tasks per minute, and total throughput is W ÷ (t + o) only until some shared stage saturates. The formula T = N × (t + o) ÷ W has no shared-stage term, so it is optimistic.
A DAG is not a bag of tasks. With dependencies the makespan cannot fall below the critical path, however many workers you add.
Keep units straight: makespan in minutes, throughput in tasks per minute; 2.67 tasks/min is 160 tasks/hour.

quiz.q: Define high-throughput computing in one sentence.
quiz.a: HTC runs many independent tasks over a pool of workers and optimises tasks completed per unit time, not the latency of one task.

quiz.q: Why must the tasks of a bag-of-tasks job be independent?
quiz.a: With no dependencies any task can go to any free worker in any order, so the master keeps every worker busy and makespan is total work divided by workers. Dependencies create idle waits and a critical path.

quiz.q: 300 tasks, 3 min each, 0.5 min overhead per task, 10 workers. Find makespan and throughput.
quiz.a: Tasks per worker = 30; time = 30 × (3 + 0.5) = 105 min; throughput = 300 ÷ 105 ≈ 2.86 tasks/min.

quiz.q: In the 600-task example, what is throughput if overhead is removed entirely?
quiz.a: Makespan = 600 × 4 ÷ 12 = 200 min; throughput = 600 ÷ 200 = 3 tasks/min, against 2.67 with overhead.

quiz.q: Explain why 24 workers would not halve the 225 min makespan if the master can only dispatch 4 tasks per minute.
quiz.a: Dispatching 600 tasks at 4 tasks/min needs 150 min. The 24 workers can do 600 × 4.5 ÷ 24 = 112.5 min of work, so work finishes before dispatch; the makespan is about 150 min, not 112.5 min. Throughput is limited by the slowest stage.

quiz.q: A workflow has tasks A → B → C, each 10 min, and 100 other independent 10 min tasks. With 4 workers, which term sets the makespan floor?
quiz.a: Chain A → B → C is the critical path at 30 min; total work 103 × 10 = 1030 min over 4 workers is 257.5 min, so makespan is about 258 min and the critical path alone does not bind.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry runs these ideas as cloud batch services and Kubernetes Jobs, and as workflow engines scheduling a DAG of containers. Search many-task computing, workflow DAG scheduling, and critical-path heuristics such as HEFT.
